newsitem.title: UK: Moody's-Bahrain's banking system faces challenges.
newsitem.headline: Moody's-Bahrain's banking system faces challenges.

text.p: Bahrain's domestic banks are in a generally good financial condition, with asset quality and profitability now much improved on levels seen in the early 1990s, Moody's Investors Service said on Monday.

"But the Bahrain banking market as whole is facing considerable challenges, in particular in the offshore sector, where Bahrain's importance as an international banking sector is declining," the rating agency said in a report.
The report is the first to be published by Moody's on the Bahrain banking system.
"Moody's rates two Bahraini commercial banks -- National Bank of Bahrain and Bank of Bahrain and Kuwait," it said.
"Both have been assigned deposit ratings of Ba2/Not Prime for their long- and short-term deposits and this reflects in part the relatively low sovereign ceiling of Ba1 assigned to Bahrain," it said.
National Bank of Bahrain has a bank financial strength rating of D plus and Bank of Bahrain and Kuwait a D rating.
These (ratings) put the banks on a par with others in nearby Kuwait, UAE, Qatar and Oman, Moody's said.
The agency said that, in terms of the number of institutions registered and the volume of assets booked, the Bahrain banking system is dominated by the offshore sector.
"The banking system also includes investment banks and branches of foreign banks. Within the on-shore sector, the two banks rated by Moody's account for more than 50 percent of the market," it said.
"It is difficult to be optimistic about the future of Bahrain as a major financial center," the report's author said.

He cited increased competition from neighboring Dubai and the fact that improved global telecommunications has rendered unnecessary the role which Bahrain hoped to play as a stepping stone in a convenient time zone between the financial markets of Asia and Europe.
The report added that recent political unrest had not helped Bahrain's cause.

As for the on-shore banks, the report said they faced the "major challenge" of how to expand their business in a limited market, particularly one which is passing through a difficult period economically and politically.

But it said banks had responded well to initiatives to encourage the introduction of collective investment schemes and that some banks have attempted to diversify their balance sheets by investing in international securities.
"Some banks have also started to take an interest in international syndications, but no domestic bank appears to have ambitions to expand its branch network internationally."
